newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel passes welfare immigrant plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel passes welfare immigrant plan.

text.p: A bitterly divided House panel on Tuesday moved to restore some federal benefits to legal immigrants affected by a new welfare law after Republicans softened some contentious provisions.

The House Ways and Means Committee, by a largely party-line vote of 21-18, approved a bill continuing federal disability aid to hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants currently on the rolls who were scheduled to be cut off this summer.

Republicans at the last minute dropped a plan to deny aid to any immigrant whose sponsor had an income of $40,000 or more. Opponents had warned that provision would have cut off benefits to many disabled immigrants.

Democrats protested that despite the change, the Republican plan would cover 125,000 fewer immigrants over 10 years than an original balanced budget deal painstakingly worked out between Congress and the White House.

By a vote of 19-20 the committee defeated a Democratic effort to continue federal benefits to all legal immigrants who were in the country before the law was signed on August 22, 1996, and may become disabled in the future.
Three Republicans voted for that amendment.

"This is not only a violation of the budget agreement that was signed by this president, but also a break in the faith of this country in caring for the sickest and weakest," said California Democratic Rep. Xavier Becerra.
Republicans argued that legal immigrants had been using the United States as a retirement home and said the federal government simply could not afford to continue aid.
"It just didn't seem right to leave in place a welfare system that was totally out of control," said Florida Republican Rep. Clay Shaw.

Democrats were also defeated when they tried to delete a provision of the bill that essentially overturns a Clinton administration plan applying minimum wage laws to welfare recipients enrolled in workfare programs.

The bill would let states count Food Stamps, cash benefits, child care, housing and medical aid when calculating hourly wages. Some governors have complained that if they paid minimum wage, they could not meet welfare work requirements.
"You put people in a situation where they in effect are being bonded. What does that do for their dignity?" asked California Democratic Rep. Pete Stark.
Republicans did alter the bill to specify that federal health and safety laws applied to workfare recipients.
A landmark welfare law signed last year ends federal benefits to most legal immigrants this summer. Clinton won major concessions in the budget agreement to "fix" the law.

Under the budget plan, legal immigrants who were in the United States by Aug. 22, 1996, and were either on the rolls because of disability or became disabled in the future could receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Medicaid.

Immigrants receiving SSI benefits because they were elderly and impoverished, rather than disabled, would have been cut off. Estimates were that about 20 percent of 700,000 immmigrants receiving SSI would lose aid.

Under the Republican plan all legal immigrants -- including the elderly poor -- receiving SSI on Aug. 22, 1996, could continue to get aid. Legal immigrants in the country on that date, but not on the rolls, would not be eligible for assistance even if they became disabled in the future.
